question: If AI agents work directly on our computers, how do we keep our private information safe?
reflection: Running AI on our own machines can give people more control over their data, as long as security grows at the same pace.

sources.subject: ChatGPT lands on Linux with Codex while Claude's hidden thinking expos

one_line: AI agents are moving onto personal computers just as researchers show that their hidden reasoning can leak private data.

top_stories.title: Hidden AI reasoning can be read out
top_stories.what: Researchers report that the scrambled reasoning some AI services return can be passed to a weaker model, which then reads it back, and public session logs held passwords and keys.
top_stories.why: Teams that share AI session logs may be exposing sensitive data without knowing it.

top_stories.title: ChatGPT arrives on Linux
top_stories.what: OpenAI released a preview desktop app for Linux that includes its coding agent, which can read local files and work inside projects.
top_stories.why: Agents with local file access need clear rules on which folders they can see.

top_stories.title: Train models on your own computer
top_stories.what: Unsloth released a free desktop app to run and fine-tune models locally on common graphics cards, with no data sent to the cloud.
top_stories.why: Local training lets researchers adapt models to sensitive data while keeping it in-house.

saudi_lens.text: Local training tools support Saudi data protection rules by keeping personal data on local machines, which helps health and government projects.

idea.title: Safe sharing check for AI logs
idea.pitch: A simple checklist and scan that finds passwords, keys and personal data in AI session logs before anyone shares them.
idea.first_step: Collect five old AI chat exports and scan them for emails and keys.

idea_kids.title: Secret note detectives
idea_kids.pitch: A game where children learn which details, like home address or passwords, should never go in a note that others might read.
idea_kids.first_step: Write ten short notes, some with private details, for children to sort into safe and not safe.
